gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: Gold works backwards. £75 is the price AFTER a 25% increase, so it equals the original times the multiplier. Find that multiplier.
steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

steps.say: The final price is original × 1.25. To get back to the original, divide instead of multiply.
steps.hint: Divide the final price by the multiplier.

steps.say: Check by going forwards: the original plus 25% should return £75.
steps.done: It lands back on £75, so the original was £60. Dividing by the multiplier is the gold move.

steps.say: One trap to avoid: taking 25% off the £75 gives a different, wrong number. See it.
steps.done: £75 − £18.75 = £56.25, which is NOT the original. Always divide by the multiplier instead.

gold.display: After a 25% increase, a coat costs £75. Find the original price.

steps.say: Bronze is one percentage change, done with a multiplier. This is an increase of 20%, so add 0.20 to 1.
steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

steps.say: Now multiply the original amount by it.
Read the answer back to be sure.
steps.hint: Subtract the original from the new price.

steps.say: And that increase should be 20% of 60.
steps.done: 12 matches, so £72 is right. That is the whole bronze move.

steps.say: Silver adds compounding: the same percentage applied several times. First the yearly multiplier for a 10% increase.
steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

steps.say: It runs for 3 years, so raise the multiplier to the power 3.
Multiply the starting amount by this single factor.
Check the interest earned looks right for 3 years.
steps.done: £662 interest on £2000 over 3 years at 10% compound. The power did the work: that is the silver move.

steps.say: No formulas yet. A £50 jacket has 10% off. 10% of £50 is £5.
That is the whole method. Taking 10% off is the same as keeping 90%, and 90% as a decimal is 0.90, so £50 × 0.90 = £45 in one step. That 0.90 is called the multiplier.
Now the twist. At the till you get a loyalty 10% off the £45 as well. 10% of £45 is £4.50.

Two 10%-offs did NOT make 20% off (that would be £40). Each cut comes off a smaller price, so they stack up: \(£50 \times 0.90 \times 0.90 = £40.50\). Raising the multiplier to a power is all compound change is.

steps: Increase of \(r\%\): multiply by \(1 + \frac{r}{100}\). Decrease: multiply by \(1 - \frac{r}{100}\).
Reverse percentage: divide the final amount by the multiplier to find the original.
Unknown rate: divide final by original, take the \(n\)th root, subtract from 1.
method_card.title: Percentages & Compound Change
method_card.content:
A multiplier turns a percentage change into one multiplication. Increase by 20% means \(\times 1.20\); decrease by 15% means \(\times 0.85\).

Compound change applies the same percentage repeatedly, so raise the multiplier to a power: \(\text{Final} = \text{Original} \times (1 \pm \frac{r}{100})^n\).

For a reverse percentage, the amount you are given is the original already multiplied, so divide by the multiplier to get back. Do not take the percentage off the final amount: it was applied to the original.
method_card.example:
A car worth £12,000 depreciates by 15% per year. Value after 3 years?

Multiplier \(= 0.85\). Value \(= 12000 \times 0.85^3 = 12000 \times 0.614125 = £7369.50\)

steps: You are given the amount AFTER a change and must work backwards. The final amount is original × multiplier, so divide by the multiplier to undo it.
For compound, divide by \((\text{multiplier})^n\). To find an unknown rate, divide final by original, take the \(n\)th root, then subtract from 1.
Never just take the percentage off the final amount: the percentage applied to the original, not the new value.
gold.title: Gold: reverse percentages and hidden rates

example.question: After a 25% increase, a coat costs £75. Find the original price.

steps: A single increase or decrease. Turn the percentage into a multiplier: an increase of \(r\%\) is \(1 + \frac{r}{100}\), a decrease is \(1 - \frac{r}{100}\).
Multiply the original amount by the multiplier. A 25% rise uses 1.25, a 30% fall uses 0.70.
Check by finding the change on its own: it should equal that percentage of the original.
bronze.title: Bronze: one percentage change

steps: The same percentage is applied again and again. Find the yearly multiplier once, exactly as in bronze.
Then raise it to the power of the number of years: \(\text{Final} = \text{Original} \times (\text{multiplier})^n\).
Two 10% rises are NOT one 20% rise: each change acts on the new amount, so always use the power, never repeated addition.
silver.title: Silver: compound change

gold.display: After a 15% increase, a TV costs £460. What was the original price?

guided_steps.say: A reverse percentage. £460 is the price AFTER a 15% increase, so it is the original times the multiplier. Find that multiplier first.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

guided_steps.say: To undo the increase, divide the final price by the multiplier.
Check by going forwards: the original plus 15% should give £460.
guided_steps.done: It lands back on £460, so the original was £400.

misconceptions.message: Divide by the multiplier: 460 ÷ 1.15 = £400. Do NOT find 15% of £460 and subtract.

gold.display: A painting decreased in value by 8% and is now worth £1,380. What was it worth before the decrease?

guided_steps.say: A reverse percentage. £1,380 is the value AFTER an 8% decrease, so it is the original times the multiplier. Find that multiplier first.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1.

guided_steps.say: To undo the decrease, divide the final value by the multiplier.
Check by going forwards: the original minus 8% should give £1,380.
guided_steps.done: It lands back on £1,380, so the original was £1,500.

misconceptions.message: Divide by the multiplier: 1380 ÷ 0.92 = £1500. Adding 8% to £1,380 (giving £1,490.40) applies the 8% to the new price, but it applied to the original.

gold.display: After 2 years of 5% compound interest, an investment is worth £5,512.50. What was the original investment?

guided_steps.say: A reverse compound problem. The final amount is the original times 1.05, twice over. First the yearly multiplier.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1.

guided_steps.say: Two years means the total factor is 1.05 squared.
Undo it by dividing the final amount by this factor.
Check by going forwards.
guided_steps.done: It lands back on £5,512.50, so the original was £5,000.

misconceptions.message: Divide by 1.05² = 1.1025: 5512.50 ÷ 1.1025 = £5000. Dividing by 1.05 only undoes one year, not two.

gold.hint: Divide final by original, take the cube root, then subtract from 1.
gold.display: A car was worth \(£16{,}000\). After 3 years at \(x\%\) depreciation it is worth \(£11{,}664\). Find the annual rate of depreciation.

guided_steps.say: First find the total factor over the 3 years: divide the final value by the original.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the final value by the starting value.

guided_steps.say: That factor is the yearly multiplier applied 3 times, so it is (multiplier) cubed. Undo the power with a cube root.
The yearly multiplier is 0.9. The rate is what was taken off each year: 1 minus the multiplier.
Turn the decimal into a percentage.
Check by going forwards: does £16,000 fall to £11,664 at 10% a year?
guided_steps.done: 16000 × 0.9 three times gives 11664. So 10% a year is right.

misconceptions.message: You have found the overall percentage drop over all three years. To find the annual rate, take the cube root of the total factor (11664 ÷ 16000), then subtract from 1 and multiply by 100.
Dividing the total loss by 3 gives the average money lost per year, not the compound rate. Depreciation multiplies each year, so take the cube root of 11664 ÷ 16000 to find the annual multiplier.
You have correctly found the annual multiplier (0.9), but the rate of depreciation is 1 minus that multiplier: 1 − 0.9 = 0.1, so the answer is 10%, not 90%.
You have divided the larger value by the smaller. Write the fraction as final ÷ original, that is 11664 ÷ 16000, then take the cube root and subtract from 1.

gold.hint: Multiply the two multipliers 0.8 and 0.9, then subtract from 1.
gold.display: A sale offers 20% off, then a further 10% off the sale price. What is the overall percentage decrease?

guided_steps.say: Two decreases one after the other. Turn each into a multiplier. First, 20% off:
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.2.

guided_steps.say: Then a further 10% off the reduced price:
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.1.

guided_steps.say: Apply both changes by multiplying the two multipliers into one overall factor.
The overall multiplier is 0.72, so 72% of the price remains. The decrease is what is missing from 1.
Turn the decimal into a percentage.

guided_steps.pre: On £100: after 20% off £80, then 10% off £80 leaves £72, so 100 − 72 =
guided_steps.say: Check with a real price of £100.
guided_steps.done: £100 falls to £72, a £28 drop, which is 28%. Not 30%.

misconceptions.message: Overall multiplier = 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72. Decrease = 1 − 0.72 = 0.28 = 28%. NOT 30%: the second 10% comes off a smaller price.

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. An increase of 25% keeps the whole amount and adds a quarter, so add 0.25 to 1.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1: 1 + 0.25.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the increase on its own should be 25% of 80.
guided_steps.done: 20 is a quarter of 80, exactly 25%. So £100 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the original from your new price.

misconceptions.message: 20 is only 25% of 80, the increase on its own. Add it back on: 80 + 20 = £100. Or multiply by 1.25 in one step.

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. A decrease of 10% keeps 90% of the amount, so take 0.1 off 1.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.1.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the amount lost should be 10% of 600.
guided_steps.done: 60 is 10% of 600. So 540 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract your answer from the original.

misconceptions.message: 60 is only 10% of 600, the amount taken off. Subtract it: 600 − 60 = 540. Or multiply by 0.9 in one step.

bronze.hint: Increase means multiply by 1.15 (or find 15% and add it on).

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. An increase of 15% adds 0.15 to 1.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1: 1 + 0.15.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the increase on its own should be 15% of 320.
guided_steps.done: 48 is 15% of 320. So £368 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the original from your new price.

misconceptions.message: 48 is only the increase (15% of 320), not the new total. Add it back on: 320 + 48 = £368. Or multiply by 1.15 in one step.

bronze.display: A shirt costs £40 and is reduced by 30%. What is the sale price?

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. Reduced by 30% leaves 70% of the price, so take 0.3 off 1.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.3.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original price by the multiplier.
Check: the reduction should be 30% of 40.
guided_steps.done: 12 is 30% of 40. So £28 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the sale price from the original.

misconceptions.message: 12 is the reduction (30% of 40), not the sale price. Take it off: 40 − 12 = £28. Or multiply by 0.7 in one step.

bronze.display: A jacket costs £180. It is reduced by 45%. What is the sale price?

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. Reduced by 45% leaves 55% of the price, so take 0.45 off 1.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.45.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original price by the multiplier.
Check: the reduction should be 45% of 180.
guided_steps.done: 81 is 45% of 180. So £99 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the sale price from the original.

misconceptions.message: 81 is the reduction (45% of 180), not the sale price. Take it off: 180 − 81 = £99. Or multiply by 0.55 in one step.

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. An increase of 40% adds 0.4 to 1.
guided_steps.hint: An increase adds the rate to 1: 1 + 0.4.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the increase should be 40% of 350.
guided_steps.done: 140 is 40% of 350. So 490 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the original from your new value.

misconceptions.message: 140 is only the increase (40% of 350), not the new total. Add it back on: 350 + 140 = 490. Or multiply by 1.4 in one step.

bronze.display: A bike costs £200 plus 20% VAT. What is the total price?

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. Adding 20% VAT adds 0.2 to 1.
Now multiply the price before VAT by the multiplier.
Check: the VAT added should be 20% of 200.
guided_steps.done: 40 is 20% of 200. So £240 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the price before VAT from the total.

misconceptions.message: 40 is only the VAT (20% of 200), not the total. Add it back on: 200 + 40 = £240. Or multiply by 1.2 in one step.

guided_steps.say: First the multiplier. A decrease of 25% keeps 75% of the amount, so take 0.25 off 1.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.25.

guided_steps.say: Now multiply the original by the multiplier.
Check: the amount lost should be 25% of 480.
guided_steps.done: 120 is a quarter of 480, exactly 25%. So 360 is right.
guided_steps.hint: Subtract your answer from the original.

misconceptions.message: 120 is only 25% of 480, the amount taken off. Subtract it: 480 − 120 = 360. Or multiply by 0.75 in one step.

silver.hint: Compound: multiply by 1.05 raised to the power 2.
silver.display: £3,000 is invested at 5% compound interest for 2 years. What is the final amount?

guided_steps.say: Compound interest is a repeated increase. First the yearly multiplier for 5%.
guided_steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

guided_steps.say: It runs for 2 years, so raise the multiplier to the power 2.
Now multiply the starting amount by this single factor.
Check the interest earned.
guided_steps.done: £307.50 interest on £3000 over 2 years at 5% compound. So £3307.50 is right.

misconceptions.message: 3000 × 1.05² = 3000 × 1.1025 = £3307.50. Adding 5% twice would give simple interest of £3300, not compound.

silver.hint: Depreciation of 20% means multiply by 0.8 each year, so use 0.8 squared.
silver.display: A car depreciates by 20% each year. It is worth £10,000 now. What will it be worth in 2 years?

guided_steps.say: Depreciation is a repeated decrease. First the yearly multiplier for 20%.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.2.

guided_steps.say: Over 2 years, raise the multiplier to the power 2.
Now multiply the current value by this factor.
Check the value lost over the 2 years.
guided_steps.done: The car lost £3600 of its £10000 value. So £6400 is right.

misconceptions.message: 10000 × 0.8² = 10000 × 0.64 = £6400. Taking off 40% in one go (£6000) ignores that the second year's 20% is smaller.

silver.display: A population of 50,000 grows by 2% per year. What is the population after 3 years? Round to the nearest whole number.

guided_steps.say: Growth is a repeated increase. First the yearly multiplier for 2%.
guided_steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

guided_steps.say: Over 3 years, raise the multiplier to the power 3.
Now multiply the starting population by this factor.

guided_steps.pre: Round to the nearest whole person:
guided_steps.say: The question asks for a whole number of people.
guided_steps.done: 53060 people after 3 years of 2% growth. That matches.

misconceptions.message: 50000 × 1.02³ = 50000 × 1.061208 = 53060. Adding 6% in one go (53000) ignores that each year grows the new, larger population.

guided_steps.say: An increase keeps the whole original (100%) and adds the extra. First write 7.5% as a decimal.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by 100: move the point two places.

guided_steps.say: An increase adds this to 1, the 100% you keep.
Check by reading it back: a multiplier of 1.075 keeps 100% and adds how much?
guided_steps.done: 7.5% extra, exactly the increase asked for. So 1.075 is right.

misconceptions.message: 1 + 0.075 = 1.075. Writing 0.075 gives only the extra bit, not the whole amount plus the extra.

silver.hint: A decrease takes away from 1: 1 minus 0.35.

guided_steps.say: A decrease keeps what is left after taking the percentage away. First write 35% as a decimal.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by 100: move the point two places.

guided_steps.say: A decrease takes this off 1, the 100% you started with.
Check: how much has been taken off?
guided_steps.done: 0.35 taken off, exactly the 35% decrease. So 0.65 is right.

misconceptions.message: 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. Writing 0.35 gives only the part removed, not the part that is left.

silver.hint: Multiply by 1.04 to the power 5, then round to the nearest pound.
silver.display: A house increases in value by 4% per year. It is currently worth £180,000. What will it be worth in 5 years? Give your answer to the nearest pound.

guided_steps.say: Growth is a repeated increase. First the yearly multiplier for 4%.
guided_steps.hint: Add the rate as a decimal to 1.

guided_steps.say: Over 5 years, raise the multiplier to the power 5.
Now multiply the current value by this factor.
The question asks for the nearest pound.
guided_steps.done: £218,998 after 5 years of 4% growth. That matches.

misconceptions.message: 180000 × 1.04⁵ = 180000 × 1.2166529 ≈ £218,998. £216,000 comes from adding 4% five times (a 20% rise), which is simple interest, not compound.

silver.hint: Multiply by 0.88 cubed, then round to the nearest penny.
silver.display: £8,000 depreciates at 12% per year for 3 years. Find the final value to the nearest penny.

guided_steps.say: Depreciation is a repeated decrease. First the yearly multiplier for 12%.
guided_steps.hint: A decrease takes the rate off 1: 1 − 0.12.

guided_steps.say: Over 3 years, raise the multiplier to the power 3.
Now multiply the starting value by this factor.
The question asks for the nearest penny.
guided_steps.done: £5451.78 left after 3 years of 12% depreciation. That matches.

misconceptions.message: 8000 × 0.88³ = 8000 × 0.681472 = £5451.78. £5120 comes from taking off 36% (12% × 3) in one go, which ignores compounding.
